title: Will ChatGPT get you caught? Rethinking of Plagiarism Detection
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether essays generated by ChatGPT can be detected as plagiarized by conventional plagiarism-detection software. The core question is whether generative AI-produced academic writing would be flagged by widely used systems, and what this implies for academic integrity in education. The study is motivated by growing concern that students may use ChatGPT to generate essays and submit them as their own work.

The authors generated 50 essays by prompting ChatGPT to write approximately 500-word essays on different topics. These outputs were then checked using two plagiarism-detection tools: Turnitin for 25 essays and iThenticate for 25 essays. As an additional exploratory step, the authors also asked ChatGPT itself whether the essays had been generated by a chatbot, treating this as a kind of reverse-engineering detection approach. The analysis focused on descriptive statistics of similarity/originality scores rather than learning outcomes or writing improvement.

No human student participants were studied; instead, the unit of analysis was AI-generated text. The context is educational assessment and academic writing, but not a classroom intervention. The paper does not report a school-based implementation, grade band, or instructional setting, and it is therefore not a direct comparative K-12 writing outcomes study.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated essays often appear highly original to standard plagiarism detectors, with most essays receiving similarity scores low enough that they might not raise concern in typical academic settings. The authors argue that conventional plagiarism detection based on text similarity may be insufficient for generative AI content, and they suggest that institutions reconsider plagiarism-detection practices and policies in light of large language models.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative descriptive study with a clearly described procedure and reported sample of 50 essays, but it is not a K-12 comparative intervention study and lacks a student sample, control group, validated outcome design, and inferential statistics. It provides limited empirical evidence on tool performance rather than educational effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests unclear but potentially meaningful institutional impact by showing that AI-generated writing may evade existing plagiarism systems, yet no student learning or writing-process effects were measured and no standardized effect sizes were reported. Impact is therefore important but empirically under-specified.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used to generate 50 short academic essays on assigned topics in order to test whether AI-generated writing could evade plagiarism-detection systems in educational settings.
Turnitin and iThenticate were used as automated plagiarism/similarity detection tools to evaluate the originality scores of ChatGPT-generated essays.
ChatGPT was additionally prompted to judge whether pasted essays were generated by a chatbot, functioning as an AI-based text-origin detector rather than as a learning support tool.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that conventional plagiarism-detection tools often rated ChatGPT-generated essays as highly original: 40 of 50 essays had similarity scores of 20% or less across Turnitin and iThenticate, suggesting these systems may fail to efficiently flag AI-generated writing. In a reverse-engineering check, ChatGPT reportedly identified 46 of 50 essays as generated by itself (>92% accuracy), outperforming the traditional similarity tools for this specific task; however, no inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or validated accuracy benchmarking were reported.
finding.measure: Plagiarism/similarity scores from Turnitin and iThenticate; count of essays identified by ChatGPT as AI-generated

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents evidence that ChatGPT can generate essays that are difficult for standard institutional plagiarism systems to detect, with 40 out of 50 essays receiving similarity scores at or below 20%. The authors interpret this as a threat to academic integrity systems and argue that institutions may need new AI-origin detection policies and revised assessment practices, but no causal institutional outcome metrics were measured.
finding.measure: Similarity/originality outcomes interpreted as implications for institutional plagiarism policy and academic integrity enforcement
